analysis.one_liner: Raises the federal minimum wage to $7.25, restores overtime pay rules, and taxes profits on imported goods to discourage offshoring.
analysis.headline: The Senate never voted on the bill: introduced January 24, 2005 with 13 Democratic cosponsors, it was referred to the Senate Finance Committee and died there when the 109th Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: This was a package of pro-worker measures: raise the federal minimum wage from $5.15 to $7.25 an hour in steps, roll back a 2004 rule that let employers deny overtime pay to more workers, require 90-day notice before companies offshore jobs, extend trade-adjustment aid to service workers, fund transportation, water, rail, and transit projects, and offer tax credits for broadband in rural and low-income areas and for research and development. It also taxes the foreign profits of US-owned corporations tied to property they import into the US. It never got past the Senate Finance Committee.
analysis.who_benefits: Roughly 7 million workers earning near the minimum wage would see phased raises to $7.25 an hour; workers reclassified as overtime-exempt under the April 2004 rule would regain overtime eligibility; employees facing offshoring would get 90-day advance notice and posted rights information; laid-off service workers would become eligible for trade adjustment assistance, including a health coverage credit; and communities with aging roads, rails, and water systems would receive new federal funding.

how_it_helps.text: Phases the federal minimum wage up from $5.15 to $5.85, then $6.55, then $7.25 an hour over roughly two years.

Nullifies the portions of the Labor Department's April 23, 2004 overtime rule that removed overtime protections from any employee who would have qualified under the pre-2003 rules, and raises the salary threshold for the executive exemption from the 1975-era $155-a-week level to $591 a week, indexed to inflation thereafter.

Adds offshoring of jobs to the Worker Adjustment and Retraining Notification Act, requiring 90 days' advance notice, posted employee-rights notices, and an annual Labor Department report on where jobs are moving.

Authorizes roughly $7 billion a year for highways, $6 billion for water systems, $1.5 billion for rail, $1.75 billion for transit, and $1.5 billion for aviation projects, with funds directed to near-term projects.

Extends trade adjustment assistance to service-sector workers, offers them enrollment in the Federal Employees Health Benefit program, improves the health coverage tax credit, and creates aid for communities hit by trade.

Allows businesses to immediately deduct broadband equipment costs when serving rural, underserved, and residential subscribers, and makes and expands the research and development tax credit permanent.
Requires trade negotiations and certification regarding China's currency valuation policy and creates a Chief Enforcement Negotiator at the US Trade Representative.

analysis.who_pays: Businesses paying the minimum wage or newly covered by overtime rules would bear higher labor costs; US-owned multinational corporations would pay a new tax on income tied to property they import; and the federal Treasury would fund tens of billions in infrastructure authorizations and forgo revenue from the broadband and research tax breaks.

drawbacks.text: The infrastructure and technology titles authorize large new federal spending without new revenue attached, adding to deficits if enacted as written.

The permanent, expanded research credit and broadband expensing are open-ended tax breaks whose main direct beneficiaries are corporations; their benefits to workers depend on companies actually hiring and investing domestically.

The minimum wage increase raises costs for small employers in low-wage sectors like restaurants and retail, and some of the package—including the multiemployer pension and free-trade statements—is only a nonbinding 'sense of the Senate' with no legal force.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The core wage and overtime provisions are direct, well-defined gains for low-paid workers at a real but limited cost to specific employers. The trade, notice, and adjustment-assistance provisions give workers practical protections against offshoring. The weakest parts are the corporate tax breaks, which are permanent revenue losses with uncertain benefits, and the several provisions that are nonbinding statements rather than law. On balance the bill's main effect is a transfer toward low-wage workers paid for by low-wage employers and the Treasury.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced and sent to the Senate Finance Committee in January 2005, and the committee never took it up, so it died when that Congress ended two years later.

narrative.text: Sen. Debbie Stabenow introduced S. 14 on January 24, 2005, joined by eleven other Democratic senators including Minority Leader Harry Reid.
The Senate read the bill twice and referred it to the Committee on Finance the same day.
No further action appears in the record: no hearings, no markup, no committee vote, and no floor vote before the 109th Congress ended on January 3, 2007.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Employers who pay the minimum wage and overtime kept the lower pre-2004 rules, multinationals avoided the new import-linked tax, and federal spending stayed flat; workers waiting on a raise got nothing.

for.name: Sen. Debbie Stabenow
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and led its Senate promotion.

for.name: Sen. Harry Reid
for.what_they_did: Was among the original senators who introduced the bill.

against.name: Senate Finance Committee
against.role: Committee of referral, chaired by Sen. Chuck Grassley (R-IA)
against.what_they_did: Received the bill on January 24, 2005 and never scheduled a hearing, markup, or vote; the bill sat until the Congress expired.

against.name: President George W. Bush
against.what_they_did: His administration issued the April 2004 overtime rule the bill would have nullified, and the bill's own findings state he proposed terminating the Advanced Technology Program the bill would reauthorize.

sides.party_line_note: Every sponsor and all 13 cosponsors were Democrats in a Senate with 55 Republicans and 44 Democrats, and the Republican-led Finance Committee never acted on the bill.

industries.note: A minimum wage rising to $7.25 and restored overtime rules directly raise their labor costs, which is exactly the money their workers would gain.
The bill adds 'imported property income' to subpart F, taxing foreign subsidiaries' profits tied to property imported into the US, and extends 90-day layoff notice to offshoring decisions.
They could immediately expense equipment serving rural, underserved, and residential subscribers, a subsidy tied to extending service where the bill's defined markets lack it.

A permanent, expanded research credit and 100% credit for contract research with small businesses, universities, and federal labs cut their tax bills; workers benefit only indirectly if the research and jobs stay onshore.

$1.5 billion a year in capital grants, conditioned on keeping collective bargaining agreements in force for work on funded corridors and treating grant-funded operators as employers under railroad labor law.
